I’ve spent the past decade asking questions for a living. I’ve spent my time finding the right people to speak to, examined evidence, worked with data and figured out how to make complex subjects accessible. Journalism gave me special moments where my sources thanked me with handwritten cards for helping open the right channels to advocate for them. Journalism has given me readers who trusted me with their most vulnerable stories. It nurtured my crusiosity and pushed me to be skeptical of easy answers. I’m proud of the work I’ve done, the skills I’ve acquired and most importantly grateful for the stories I’ve been given the honour to tell.

Here comes the infamous “but.” I’m still looking to leave. It oddly feels like an apology letter and perhaps it is one- to myself and the hopes I weaved as a teenager picking journalist to be my vocation for life. Life happens. World changed. Heck, we have a whole new being (ahmm AI) to be competing with.

I’ve been asking myself a set of questions journalism can’t quite answer, or fit in the puzzle to. Am I still learning at the pace I want to? Is there room for me to develop the skills I’m excited about? Can I see a path ahead that is both fulfilling and sustainable? Increasingly, my answer has been that I need to look beyond journalism, unfortunately.

This is a considered decision, not a sudden loss of faith in this work. I still believe journalism matters. I still care about the quality of information people encounter and the way important stories are told. But it would be naïve of me to keep believing in the traditional newsroom setup as the most sustainable way forward for it.

The most immediate reason is growth. Newsrooms can be slow, bureaucratic and averse to new ideas. Cue this: When the world moved to mostly consuming information (and entertainment) digitally, many journalists held on to the old glory of wanting their name in print. It feels more tangible, I get it. I’ve been guilty of the temptation too. For years, the tussle between publishing digitally and in print continued only to eventually be won out by the electronic side, after much hesitation and resistance. When the switch happened, it was abrupt, not thought out and truthfully, too late. The internet made mass media accessible, something the news industry should have been proud of and embraced to its advantage, but respectfully failed to find ways to survive in.

Authorship evolved further with social media and newsrooms didn’t keep up, often out of sheer arrogance considering ourselves the pallbearers of information dissemination. Numbers held a rude mirror. Globally, jobs in the industry are shrinking, salaries have laid dormant and despite many rounds of auditing workforce, the top has remained heavily paid while talented reporters and editors are let go.

A few years ago, I made a small pivot within the industry, choosing the side of data-led storytelling, learning large-scale data collection, analysis and frontend development. I now sit between two disciplines – storytelling, like the old days, but using tools that are contemporary.

My reporting days helped me connect with people on deep, personal levels. My information designer days have been rewarding in a different way – I’m constantly challenged to expand my tech stack, find better ways to communicate the stories we’re telling and keep up.

I’ve enjoyed this. I want more of this. I want to deepen my technical skills, work with emerging technologies and learn from people whose expertise is different from my own, who will push me to learn more. I’m particularly interested in how artificial intelligence can help people work with information, make better decisions and understand complicated systems- I guess in some ways, I’m still a journalist in my heart. I want to use AI in objective ways, as a tool and not necessarily let it independently think for me.

I want the time, support and opportunity to explore those questions seriously, rather than fit learning into whatever space is left after the day’s immediate demands. A lot of the learning and experimentation I want to do requires sustained attention, which isn’t often a luxury in newsrooms.

Journalism is navigating changes in technology, audience behaviour and business models and under these pressures, newsrooms don’t fare well in giving its employees the deserved quality of life and financial motivations. The questions facing the industry are not new, and they will not have simple answers. But they do affect the choices available to people working within it.

I don’t say this to dismiss the people doing important work, but politically motivated pressures have tarnished the industry beyond repair. Many journalists I know will find ways to do ambitious work despite the challenges and I admire that commitment. I’m pregnant and my career lately hasn’t been a source of joy to me. My child deserves better than that.

The decision to leave is also about recognising that my experience will have more to offer elsewhere. Over the past ten years, I’ve learned how to investigate unfamiliar subjects and communicate findings with clarity. I’ve worked with data from collection through to analysis and presentation. I’ve built visual and interactive ways to tell stories, and I’ve learned to think about what audiences and stakeholders need to feel more equipped in their decision making- whether it is voters picking a candidate or lawmakers weighing the merits of different proposed policies.

Tech companies, product development and artificial intelligence all need people who can make sense of complexity, consider the human implications of decisions and communicate clearly. I know that moving into a new field will require me to learn a great deal and I’m ready (and excited!) for that.
I want to find work that draws on my strengths while stretching me in new directions. I want to be made uncomfortable and then to solve hurdles. I want to be around people who challenge how I think.
Leaving journalism will be a significant change. It has shaped how I see the world.
After ten years of asking questions for my work, I’m ready to act on the answers I’ve found along the way.
